deep_dive_html:
The Perils of Discretionary Relocation

In the industrial and logistics sector, a relocation clause is not merely a logistical inconvenience; it is a fundamental threat to operational continuity. Landlords often insert 'kick-out' provisions that grant them the unilateral right to move a tenant to a different unit within the same development. While seemingly benign, these clauses are frequently drafted with extreme landlord discretion, allowing for the displacement of tenants into spaces that lack the critical infrastructure necessary for modern logistics operations.

The primary danger lies in the lack of technical specificity regarding the replacement space. A landlord may move a tenant from a premium site featuring 36-foot clear heights, heavy-duty floor slabs, and extensive yard depth to a secondary space with 2-foot lower ceilings, inferior loading bay configuration, and restricted maneuvering radii. Such a move can render your existing racking systems obsolete, necessitate expensive capital expenditures for new equipment, and cripple your throughput capacity, effectively forcing a de facto lease termination under the guise of a relocation.

Establishing Market-Standard Protections

To mitigate this risk, a sophisticated tenant must negotiate strict 'comparability' standards that go beyond mere square footage. A robust relocation defense requires the following protections:

  • Technical Specification Parity: The replacement space must match or exceed the current space's clear height, dock door count, loading bay configuration, and floor load capacity.
  • Operational Continuity Protections: The lease must mandate that the landlord bears all costs associated with the move, including specialized equipment relocation, IT/infrastructure reconfiguration, and any documented business interruption or downtime.
  • Geographic and Access Constraints: Relocation should be restricted to spaces within a defined radius and must maintain equivalent access to major highways, rail spurs, or intermodal hubs.
  • Right of Refusal: Tenants should retain the right to reject any space that fails to meet the pre-defined technical criteria, with the option to terminate the lease if no suitable space is available.
